summary: Proposes a model for describing routing in the Internet, adapted from the OSI Routeing Framework, built around administrative domains and routing domains. It does not specify an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Networks belong to different owners. This offers a way to draw the boundaries and talk about who controls which roads.

subtitle: A better way to model how the Internet organizes routing and administration.

tldr.problem: The Internet's growth had outgrown the original Autonomous System model, which assumed a single routing protocol per AS and a clear hierarchical structure. Real networks often mix multiple routing protocols and have complex administrative boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes the Administrative Domain/Routing Domain (AD/RD) model from the OSI Routing Framework: Administrative Domains group systems by management authority, and within each AD, Routing Domains group systems by routing policy. This separates administrative ownership from routing strategy.
tldr.outcome: The AD/RD model provided a clearer conceptual framework for understanding large, complex networks. It remained influential in routing architecture but this RFC is Informational, not standards-track.

facts.label: AD nesting
facts.value: Can be hierarchical but not required

facts.label: RD scope
facts.value: Must be within a single AD

today: This RFC is Informational and does not specify an Internet standard. It remains an influential conceptual model, though the Autonomous System model is more commonly referenced. Modern Internet routing still reflects many of the principles outlined here, particularly the separation of administrative and routing concerns.

sections.title: Overview and Motivation
sections.content:
The Internet's original routing model used Autonomous Systems (AS), which assumed a single administrative authority running a consistent routing protocol with full mutual trust. This model worked well when the Internet was smaller, but by the late 1980s, the explosive growth had created situations the AS model did not describe well.

This RFC proposes the Administrative Domain/Routing Domain (AD/RD) model, adapted from the OSI Routing Framework. The model separates two distinct concepts: Administrative Domains (who manages the network) and Routing Domains (how routing is done). This separation better matches the reality of large regional networks and national backbones, which often contain multiple routing protocols and multiple administrative jurisdictions.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way thought of each network as having one boss and one routing protocol. The new model says networks have bosses (Administrative Domains) and routing teams (Routing Domains), and they don't have to be the same. A big company might have one boss but different departments using different routing systems.

sections.title: Key Concepts and Terminology
sections.content:
Administrative Domain (AD): A collection of End Systems (hosts), Intermediate Systems (routers), and subnetworks operated by a single organization or administrative authority. Components within an AD trust each other significantly, but interact with other ADs in a mutually suspicious manner. From outside, an AD appears as a cohesive entity whose internal structure is unimportant.

Routing Domain (RD): A set of End Systems and Intermediate Systems that operate according to the same routing procedures (same metrics, metric techniques, information distribution protocol, and path computation algorithm). All routers in an RD can determine whether another system within the domain is reachable and can compute paths to it. A Routing Domain is wholly contained within a single Administrative Domain.

Common Domain (CD): An Administrative Domain at the highest level that does not belong to any higher domain. In the Internet, this is analogous to national peer backbones. Multiple Common Domains cooperate to route globally.
sections.plainLanguage: Administrative Domains are organizations (who's in charge). Routing Domains are teams using the same routing method. A Routing Domain can't span two organizations, but an organization can have multiple routing teams. Common Domains are the top-level peers like national backbones.

sections.title: Structure and Three Types of Routing
sections.content:
The OSI Routing Framework classifies routing into three types:

  • Intra-Routing Domain routing (interior): High mutual trust; systems share the same routing protocol and information distribution. Complex tightly-coupled procedures work well here.
  • Intra-Administrative Domain routing (between routing domains): Moderate trust; multiple routing domains must be interconnected within one administration. The connection ranges from tightly coupled to more policy-based.
  • Inter-Administrative Domain routing (exterior): Low trust; systems across different organizations must manage information flow strictly. Concerns are administrative (legal, political, security, access control). Multiple agreements between different administrations are not transitive.

Routing Domains may be recursively subdivided into Subdomains to reduce routing complexity and hide details from other subdomains. Administrative Domains can be organized into a loose hierarchy that reflects availability and authoritativeness of routing information.
sections.plainLanguage: Three levels of communication: within a team (high trust), between teams in one organization (medium trust), and between organizations (low trust, formal agreements needed).

sections.title: Mapping the Model to the Real Internet
sections.content:
The AD/RD model maps well to the Internet of the late 1980s and 1990s:

  • National backbones (NSFNET, ARPANET, MILNET, and others) function as Common Domains, each with sufficient global routing knowledge to reach any Internet address.
  • Regional networks are Administrative Domains with multilateral policy agreements between each other and the backbones.
  • Campus and local networks are Routing Domains or Subdomains within a regional AD.
  • A classic Autonomous System becomes a congruent AD and RD—a single administrative authority with a single routing protocol.

However, many real Autonomous Systems diverge from this ideal. Large regional networks often act as single ADs while containing multiple RDs running different IGPs internally. This flexibility is one reason the AD/RD model better describes real networks than the strict AS model.
sections.plainLanguage: Big national networks are the top peers. Regional networks are organizations. Campuses are departments. What used to be called an 'Autonomous System' is now seen as a special case where one organization runs one routing method.

sections.title: Practical Benefits and Dual Protocol Internet
sections.content:
The AD/RD model provides practical benefits for engineering large networks. Because a Routing Domain cannot span multiple Administrative Domains, network engineers must make clear policy choices: if a campus wants its own routing policy, it becomes a separate AD. The model prevents problematic arrangements like splitting a Routing Domain across multiple ADs.

The model also permits what the strict AS model forbade: multiple IGPs within a single AD. This flexibility matches real deployments where regional networks successfully run different routing protocols in different areas, all coordinated by a single administration.

As the Internet transitioned to dual protocol operation (TCP/IP and OSI), the RFC notes that the same AD/RD boundaries would apply to both protocol suites, providing a unified, manageable routing environment. The AD/RD model became the conceptual foundation for this dual-protocol internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The model helps engineers make clear decisions about where to draw administrative and routing boundaries. It also lets one organization use different routing methods in different parts of its network, which the old Autonomous System model didn't allow. When the Internet started running both old and new protocols, the same AD/RD boundaries worked for both.
